{"filename":"06a_cache_and_ledger_essay_README.md","content_type":"text/markdown","size_bytes":21188,"content":"# SOURCE FILE: cache-and-ledger/README.md (verbatim copy, author: Yahya Efe Kuruçay)

# The Cache and the Ledger

*Why LLM-maintained knowledge bases keep failing, and the one shape that doesn't.*

---

I set out to build a thing a lot of people are building right now: a knowledge base an LLM both writes and reads. Typed docs, a compiler that keeps them honest against the code, a CLI that hands an agent exactly the context it needs so it stops flailing through `glob`/`grep`/`read` on every task. The pitch writes itself. Context bloat is real, agents waste turns rediscovering the same files, and a well-kept knowledge layer sounds like the fix.

I spent about a million tokens of research trying to break the idea before building it. It broke. But it broke in a specific, useful way — it split cleanly into one half that is a forty-year graveyard and one half that five unrelated systems independently reinvented. This is the writeup.

The one-sentence version:

> **If a fact can be derived from a source of truth, it is a cache — don't store it, regenerate it. If it cannot be derived, it is a decision — store it, once, forever. Almost every failed knowledge system failed by confusing the two.**

---

## The thing everyone actually wants

State it plainly, because the wanting is legitimate. You want a knowledge layer that:

- an LLM maintains, so humans don't rot it;
- never bloats the context window with noise;
- is as deterministic as possible, with the irreducibly fuzzy part — and *only* that part — left to the model;
- answers questions *and* gets written as a byproduct of work.

Nothing about that is unreasonable. The trouble starts the moment you try to make one artifact do all of it, because the artifact contains two kinds of sentence that have opposite physics.

---

## Two kinds of sentence

Take one real doc from a real codebase — a page describing an FAQ feature. It contains sentences like these:

**Derivable:**
- "Storage is `B2C_Faq` plus a localization table, with items in `B2C_FaqItem`."
- "The controller lives at `Controllers/Cms/B2C/FaqController.cs`."
- "It reuses the shared rich-text sanitizer."

**Not derivable:**
- "FAQ is a dedicated entity that *owns its items* — it is deliberately **not** a content block with a convention on top."

The first three are re-derivable from the code. If the doc and the code disagree, the code wins, trivially, and a machine can regenerate the sentence from scratch. They are a **cache** of the code.

The last one cannot be recovered from the code, because the code does not contain the road not taken. "We considered making this a content block and rejected it" is *intent*. It lives nowhere in the artifact it describes. It is a **decision**.

Once you see the split, you can't unsee it, and it explains every failure below.

| Symptom | What actually happened |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes KEP `replaces:` — of 50 forward values, **3 resolve**, 47 are junk (URLs, dead paths) | a typed field that gates nothing decays into freetext |
| Python PEP back-links **64% reciprocal** (27/42) | `Superseded-By` was derivable, stored anyway |
| Doc `updated:` dates silently lie | git already knows; copied anyway |
| Literate programming died | narrative "how it works" was derivable, hand-written anyway |
| ADRs write-once ~47–57% (67 repos, 765 ADRs) | **not a bug — correct.** Decisions don't change; they get superseded |

That last row is the tell. When people first measure ADR repos and find half the records are never edited after creation, they read it as neglect. It isn't. A decision *should* be write-once. The things that rot are the things that were derivable and got frozen into storage anyway.

---

## Why the cache half is a graveyard

I went looking for anyone who made "LLM keeps the derivable half in sync" actually work. Here is the tour.

**Literate programming (1984–).** Knuth's own 1984 paper pre-conceded the adoption problem, and the failure repeats for forty years with suspicious regularity: pbrt ships plain C++ and writes the literate book separately; lcc's living version diverged from its literate one; Axiom ripped out its literate tooling in 2014; TeX is literate *and deliberately frozen*. The pattern is unmistakable — **literate coupling survives exactly where change stops.** Eve, the strongest literate system ever built, removed every tooling excuse (no tangle step, live, treated prose/code mismatch as a compile error) and still failed on the only thing that mattered: *"people didn't actually like writing a bunch of prose."* Coupling docs to code doesn't fail because the coupling breaks. It fails because the coupling holds — it taxes the one thing you most want to stay cheap, refactoring.

**Swimm ($33M, patented auto-sync).** The closest commercial attempt. Its anchoring is fuzzy diff-matching with git-blame as a tiebreaker; above a change threshold it gives up and flags the doc "Outdated" for a human. It did not solve the rename problem — it built a triage queue around it. Five years, no Series B, and its homepage now sells *"agentic modernization"* consulting with "senior engineers to catch what tools miss." The strongest evidence against the model is Swimm's own current homepage: they re-inserted the human as the product.

**DeepWiki, Mintlify, Cursor docs (LLM-generated).** No vendor — first-party or independent — claims anyone treats these as ground truth without human review. Every one hedges to "draft, then review." One independent audit of DeepWiki found factual errors in every section examined and a setup instruction to install a **VS Code extension that does not exist**. Confident and wrong is worse than stale: a stale doc degrades gracefully because you half-trust it; a fluent hallucination you fully trust.

**GraphRAG (Microsoft).** Building the index costs ~375× a plain vector index [research figure — verify before publishing]. The global-summary architecture means one new document can force re-summarizing communities it never touched — an invalidation cascade. Microsoft closed the incremental-update issue in January 2026 with, essentially, *we're not building this; re-index and rely on the cache.* Their own fix, LazyGraphRAG, defers all the LLM work to query time — i.e. removes the cache.

**Agent memory (Mem0, Zep, Letta…).** A 32-day production audit of one system found **97.8% junk** — including a hallucinated "prefers Vim" fact that the pipeline re-ingested from its own memory into 808 duplicates. That feedback loop is exactly the shape of "an LLM that both writes and reads its own store."

And underneath all of it, the base rate: independent measurement puts even GPT-4 code comments at **~20% factually wrong** [research figure — verify], and automated detection of whether generated prose is hallucinated tops out around ROC-AUC 0.6 — barely above a coin flip. You cannot cheaply verify the cache you are generating.

---

## Three reasons the cache half is not just hard but wrong

The graveyard is empirical. Three independent results say it's structural.

**1. Lens theory.** The database "view-update problem" (1981) and Pierce's lens laws formalize when a derived view can be edited and pushed back to its source. The condition is strict, and prose documentation fails it structurally, not just in practice: docs are not a lossy-but-recoverable view of code — they *add* information (rationale, tradeoffs) that isn't in the code at all. A transform that isn't even a function of its source has no inverse to invert. The one place teams achieve real sync (Fern generating API docs from an OpenAPI schema) works by **eliminating the human edit surface** — the doc becomes a pure regenerable projection with no independent content. That is the cache/decision split, restated by the theory: derivable views can be kept in sync by *deleting them and regenerating*; anything with independent content cannot.

**2. Determinism.** Every incremental build system that avoids redundant work — Bazel, Salsa (rust-analyzer), Roslyn's incremental generators — relies on *early cutoff*: recompute a node, and if the new output equals the old, stop the invalidation there. The rustc docs state the precondition as a hard requirement: same inputs *must* yield the same output "or else the compiler is not deterministic." An LLM does not clear that bar. It does not emit byte-identical prose for identical input, so the equality check never fires, and cutoff silently degrades to *recompute everything, every time*. There is no published system doing principled early cutoff over non-deterministic outputs. "Semantically equal even if not byte-equal" exists only as best-effort LLM caching that knowingly serves wrong answers for latency — precisely what a correctness-bearing knowledge base cannot accept.

**3. Metacrap, automated.** Doctorow's 2001 "Metacrap" lists seven reasons self-asserted metadata is unreliable. An LLM asserting the metadata kills the shallow four (it isn't lazy, has no incentive to lie) — but leaves the deep three untouched (a schema still isn't neutral; there's still more than one way to describe a thing) and *invents an eighth*: confident fabrication with no epistemic state corresponding to "I don't actually know this." A lying human knows they lied. A lazy human knows they skipped it. The model's errors correlate with no legible signal — they're statistically indistinguishable in surface form from correct output — which makes them *harder* to catch than the human failure modes we built filters for.

---

## Why the decision half is solid

Now the other half — and the surprise. The "store only decisions, write-once, forward-links-only, derive the back-links, resolve supersession by rule not judgment" design is not something I invented. Five unrelated lineages converged on it under different pressure, which is about as strong as design evidence gets.

- **Datomic** implements "store the forward reference, derive the reverse on the fly" as a *language feature*, and documents it in almost those exact words.
- **Git** stores each commit's parent pointer and derives "children" by scanning — because storing the reverse "would undermine the immutability of past commits."
- **IETF RFCs**: the new document declares what it `Obsoletes`; the old document is *never touched*, and "obsoleted-by" lives only in a derived index.
- **ADRs** (Nygard): you don't edit an accepted record; *"the truth of the architecture is the full chain, not the latest one."*
- **Double-entry bookkeeping**, 13th century: entries are append-only, and **balances are never stored** — they're summed on demand, because storing them invites divergence. "Accountants don't use erasers."

The shared move every time: **never store a derived value next to its source.** Store the forward-written, non-derivable fact; compute everything else. It's the same instinct as computing an account balance instead of caching it.

**The asymmetry is real, and it's measured first-hand — but its magnitude depends on the regime.** The forward link (written by an author already in the file) survives; the back link (an edit to a document you're not otherwise touching) lags. How much it lags tracks how hard the process gates the field:

| Dataset | forward | back / reciprocity | regime |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python PEPs (733) | 42 `Replaces` | 27 reciprocated — **64%** | CI linter checks the header |
| Kubernetes KEPs (656) | 50 `replaces` (3 resolve) | 4 `status: replaced` | field gates nothing → near-total decay |
| ADR population (67 repos, 765) | 50 forward | 22 back — **2.3 : 1** | ordinary hand-kept records |

So the gap is not the order-of-magnitude one an earlier research pass reported ("back-links ~3.7%, forward far more common") — across a real 67-repo ADR population the forward reference is only ~2.3× the back, and back-references *are* genuinely maintained in 16 of 67 repos. **But in every regime the back-link is incompletely maintained** — 36% missing even under a linter, almost entirely gone where nothing checks it. That is the whole argument for *deriving* the back-link instead of storing it: derive it and it is 100% by construction, in every regime, for free.

And it explains the one number that looked like decay. In the most disciplined decision system in existence — Python PEPs — the forward link (`Replaces`, written by the author already editing their doc) reciprocates at **27/42 (64%)**, while the back-link direction (`Superseded-By`, requiring you to go edit a document you're not otherwise touching) sits at 84% — with 10 PEPs carrying a `Superseded-By` header while their status disagrees. The weaker-reciprocated direction is exactly the one that forces an edit to an untouched document. The fix isn't discipline. It's to **stop storing the back-link and derive it** — then the gap cannot exist by construction.

*(That 64% is not taken on faith. `data/verify-pep-reciprocity.py` downloads the public PEP dataset and computes it first-hand — 733 PEPs, 42 forward relations across 36 PEPs, 27 reciprocated. Re-run it and you get the same number, or a newer one.)*

---

## The taxes you actually sign up for

Convergence doesn't mean free. Append-only, decision-only systems have a well-documented bill, and honesty requires naming it:

- **Schema evolution is a permanent tax.** The moment you add a field non-authors must interpret, you owe an upcaster, forever. Every mature event-sourced system pays this.
- **Deletion collides with reality.** "Never delete" meets GDPR and "this was recorded in error." Datomic's excision triggers massive index rewrites and its own team says use it rarely. Design the redaction path *before* you need it, because every system that didn't, bolted it on later at real cost. `bin/ledger redact` is that path: it tombstones a record's content while preserving its id and supersession links, so every derived back-link survives — the one narrow write-once exception, designed in, not bolted on.
- **No free self-check.** Double-entry catches its own corruption only because the domain has an invariant (debits = credits). Decisions have no such checksum. If you want "the system catches its own rot," you build it deliberately — e.g. a validator that supersession chains stay acyclic and single-headed.

These are affordable at decision-log volume. They are not zero.

---

## What this leaves you building

Strip everything the research killed and here's the residue — deliberately tiny, and small *is the point*:

1. **A decision log.** Write-once records of the non-derivable "why." Forward links only. Supersession resolved by `max(serial)` in code, never by asking a model which fact is newer — because the one benchmark built to test that ("don't ask the LLM to track freshness") found deterministic resolution beats LLM judgment by 10+ points, widening under load.

2. **Do not store the derivable half at all.** Let the agent read the code. On code, agentic `grep`/`read` is competitive precisely because code has structure to exploit — unique identifiers, call graphs. (Caveat worth stating: that structure is exactly what docs *lack*, so retrieval over a prose corpus is a genuinely harder and more open question than "just grep it." But the corpus that survives here — decisions — is small.)

3. **An immune system, not a certifier.** The one automatable check is cheap and worth running in CI: does every `file:symbol` anchor still resolve? But resolving proves the file exists, not that the claim is true — and a *validated* anchor makes a stale claim sound **more** authoritative, not less. So it flags, it doesn't bless. Detecting drift is a solved research problem (~90%+); preventing it without a human is not. Budget drift as expected maintenance, not a bug to engineer away.

Everything else — typed frontmatter migrations, a `related:` graph, stored `updated:` fields, an LLM-regenerated cache, semantic-equality invalidation — is a thing someone already tried and buried. The residue is a ledger and a linter. That's the whole product, and its smallness is the finding.

---

## Run it

Two Bash scripts, no dependencies. `bin/anchor-check` is the immune system; `bin/ledger` is the decision log. Point them at a real repo.

```
$ bin/anchor-check path/to/wiki path/to/code-root
rooted anchors: 315 | resolve: 315 | broken: 0
unrooted mentions (not verifiable, discipline gap): 296
clean: every rooted anchor resolves.
```

That output is the whole thesis in three lines. On a real 120-doc wiki, **315 code references are fully-qualified addresses and every one resolves** — but **296 more are bare mentions** (`FaqDtos.cs`, `components/Foo.tsx`), which no machine can verify because they aren't addresses. Anchor discipline exists in theory and is half-kept in practice, and the tool tells you exactly which half. It flags a broken *address* as drift (exit 1); it stays silent on truth, because truth isn't machine-checkable.

```
$ bin/ledger new decisions/ "FAQ owns its items" --supersedes 2
$ bin/ledger show decisions/ --all
* 0001  Media stored as path hierarchy            [current]
  0002  FAQ modelled as content block             (superseded by 0004)
* 0004  FAQ owns its items                        [current]

$ grep -rl superseded_by decisions/     # nothing — back-links are derived, never stored
```

The `(superseded by 0004)` on record 2 was never written into any file. Record 2 is immutable; nobody edited it when 4 arrived. The back-link is *derived by scanning*, exactly like Git derives a commit's children — which is why the PEP-style 36% reciprocity gap cannot exist here by construction.

---

## Coda

I started wanting a clever compiler. I ended with an accountant's ledger and a `grep` loop in CI. The disappointment is the result: the interesting move wasn't a mechanism, it was a *cut* — the line between what a machine can re-derive and what only a human ever decided. Everything on the derivable side wants to be recomputed, not stored. Everything on the decision side wants to be stored once and never touched. The forty-year graveyard is full of systems that ran that line through the middle of a single artifact and then spent themselves trying to keep both halves in sync.

Don't keep them in sync. Keep them apart.

---

### On the numbers

Three tiers, honestly labelled:

- **Verified first-hand, reproducible.** Four scripts, all against live data or a real repo, all re-runnable:
  - `bin/anchor-check` — 315/315 rooted anchors resolve vs 296 unverifiable bare mentions (real 120-doc wiki); 8/8 ADR statuses at 1/1 reciprocity in that wiki.
  - `data/verify-pep-reciprocity.py` — 733 PEPs; forward reciprocity 27/42 (64%), back 27/32 (84%), 10 header/status mismatches.
  - `data/verify-kep-decay.py` — 656 KEPs; 50 forward `replaces` values, only 3 resolvable, vs 4 `status: replaced`.
  - `data/verify-adr-writeonce.py` + the 67-repo sweep in `data/adr-sweep-results.md` — 765 ADRs across 67 repos: write-once **46.5%** pooled / **56.6%** per-repo (the "~52%" claim sits between them, confirmed), 68% carry a status field, and **50 forward vs 22 back** supersede references (2.3:1) with every SHA recorded for replay.

  Three of these came out *different from* the research pass, each caught by re-measuring: the KEP decay was sharper (3/50 resolvable, not "44 real"); MADR's status count was 3/19 not 1/19 (the agent even claimed ADR-0008 "Add Status Field" carries no status — it carries `status: on hold`); and the ADR supersede asymmetry is 2.3:1, **not** the order-of-magnitude "3.7% back-links" the pass reported. That is three fabrication-shaped errors from an automated pass, all corrected only because the numbers live behind scripts.
- **Agent-reported, not yet re-verified** (marked "verify before publishing"): GraphRAG's ~375× index cost; the ~20% comment-error rate. These remain claims until a script reproduces them.
- **The discipline this enforces:** an LLM asserting a number is Metacrap obstacle #8 — confident fabrication with no epistemic state for "I didn't actually check." The only defense is to make the check cheap and reproducible, which is what the scripts are for. Everything not behind a script stays a claim, not a fact.

---

## What's in here

```
README.md   this essay
PAPER.md    the same argument as an empirical note (arXiv-shaped draft)
bin/
  anchor-check   the immune system — flags broken code anchors, never blesses truth
  ledger         the decision log — write-once, forward-links, derived back-links, redact
data/
  verify-pep-reciprocity.py   PEP forward/back reciprocity, live dataset
  verify-kep-decay.py         KEP typed-field decay
  verify-adr-writeonce.py     ADR write-once + supersede asymmetry
  README.md                   how to reproduce every number
decisions/  this project's own decisions, kept in its own ledger (dogfood)
test.sh     every tool control paired with its falsifier (15 checks)
```

Run the tools' self-test: `./test.sh` (15 passed, 0 failed — each control has a paired failure case, because a check that cannot fail only looks like it works).
"}

{"filename":"06b_cache_and_ledger_paper_decisions_tools.md","content_type":"text/markdown","size_bytes":30501,"content":"# SOURCE FILE: cache-and-ledger/PAPER.md (verbatim copy)

# Store the Decision, Derive the Rest: An Empirical Note on Why Knowledge Bases Rot Asymmetrically

*Draft — empirical note. Every quantitative claim is backed by a re-runnable script in `data/`; numbers still marked [UNVERIFIED] are pending first-hand reproduction and must not be cited as fact.*

## Abstract

Systems that couple documentation to code — from literate programming to LLM-maintained wikis — fail with striking regularity. We argue the failures share one cause: a single artifact is made to hold two kinds of statement with opposite maintenance physics. **Derivable** statements ("the controller is `FaqController.cs`") are recoverable from a source of truth and should be regenerated, never stored; **decision** statements ("we rejected modelling this as a content block") are not recoverable from any artifact and must be stored, once. We give a decidability argument for why the derivable half cannot be kept in sync automatically (lens theory, determinism, and an LLM-specific failure mode), and we measure the decision half's characteristic rot — an asymmetry between forward and back references — first-hand across three public corpora (Python PEPs, Kubernetes KEPs, and a set of ADR repositories). In every corpus the forward reference (written by an author already editing the document) is populated far more reliably than the back reference (which demands an edit to an untouched document). The design implication is a two-line system: an append-only decision ledger whose back-links are *derived*, and a linter that flags broken code anchors without ever asserting a document is true. We ship both as ~330 lines of dependency-free shell.

## 1. Two kinds of sentence

Take one documentation page describing a software feature. It contains, intermixed:

- *Derivable:* "Storage is table `B2C_Faq`; the controller is `FaqController.cs`; it reuses the shared sanitizer." Each is a fact about code, recoverable from the code. If page and code disagree, the code wins; a machine can regenerate the sentence.
- *Decision:* "This is a dedicated entity that owns its items — deliberately **not** a content block with a convention on top." This is intent. The rejected alternative exists nowhere in the code. It can be recorded but never recomputed.

We call the first a **cache** of the source of truth and the second a **decision**. The claim of this note is that most documentation-rot pathologies are the two being stored in one place and maintained under one policy.

## 2. Why the cache half cannot be automated

Three independent arguments, each pointing the same way.

**Lens theory / the view-update problem.** A derived view can be edited and pushed back to its source only for a restricted class of transformations (well-behaved lenses; Bancilhon–Spyratos 1981; Foster et al. 2007). Prose documentation is not in that class: it does not merely project the code, it *adds* information (rationale, tradeoffs) absent from the code. A transform that is not a function of its source has no inverse. The systems that achieve real doc↔code sync (e.g. API docs generated from an OpenAPI schema) do so by removing the independent edit surface — the doc becomes a pure regenerable projection with no content of its own. That is exactly the cache/decision split, restated by the theory.

**Determinism.** Every incremental build system that avoids redundant work (Bazel's change-pruning, Salsa's red-green backdating, Roslyn's incremental generators) depends on *early cutoff*: recompute a node, and if its output equals the prior output, halt propagation. The rustc documentation states the precondition as a hard requirement — identical inputs *must* yield identical output "or else the compiler is not deterministic." LLM generation does not satisfy this: it does not emit byte-identical prose for identical input, so the equality check never fires and cutoff degrades to full recomputation. We found no published system performing sound early cutoff over non-deterministic node outputs; "semantically equal but not byte-equal" exists only as best-effort caching that knowingly serves stale answers — unacceptable for a correctness-bearing store.

**An LLM-specific failure mode.** Doctorow's "Metacrap" (2001) lists why self-asserted metadata is unreliable. An LLM asserting metadata removes the incentive-and-effort obstacles (it is not lazy, has no motive to lie) but leaves the structural ones (a schema is not neutral) and adds a new one: confident fabrication with no epistemic state corresponding to "I did not actually verify this." Independent measurement puts even strong models' code-comment factual-error rate near 20% [UNVERIFIED — pending first-hand reproduction], and automated detection of hallucinated technical prose near chance. The cache you generate cannot be cheaply verified.

## 3. The decision half: measured rot is asymmetric

Decisions are correctly write-once — a decision does not change, it is superseded. The characteristic failure is therefore not editing but *linking*: a new decision must reference what it replaces (forward), and ideally the replaced decision references its replacement (back). We measured this asymmetry first-hand.

**Method.** For each corpus we obtained the public dataset, parsed the forward reference field (`Replaces` / `replaces` / `supersedes`) and the back reference or stored-back-state (`Superseded-By` / `status: replaced`), and computed reciprocity. Scripts are in `data/`; each hits live data and is re-runnable.

**Results.**

| Corpus | N | Forward references | Back / reciprocity | Regime | Script |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Python PEPs | 733 | 42 `Replaces` (36 PEPs) | 27 reciprocated = **64%**; back-dir 27/32 = 84%; 10 mismatches | CI linter checks header | `verify-pep-reciprocity.py` |
| Kubernetes KEPs | 656 | 50 `replaces`, **3 resolve** (47 junk) | 4 `status: replaced` | field gates nothing | `verify-kep-decay.py` |
| ADR population | 765 / 67 repos | 50 forward supersede refs | 22 back = **2.3 : 1** | ordinary hand-kept records | `verify-adr-writeonce.py` + sweep |

The direction requiring an edit to an untouched document is the one that lags — but the *magnitude* is regime-dependent, and this corrects an earlier automated pass that reported the ADR gap as near-total (back ~3.7%). Measured first-hand across 67 repos, forward is only ~2.3× back, and back-references are genuinely maintained in 16 of 67 repos. The asymmetry sharpens exactly where the process stops checking: near-perfect maintenance would need a gate, and Kubernetes' ungated `replaces` field has instead decayed almost entirely into unresolvable freetext (3 of 50 values resolve) — *a typed field that nothing validates degenerates.* In every regime the back-link is incompletely maintained; deriving it makes it complete by construction, for free.

**Write-once rate.** Measured across 765 ADRs in 67 repositories (`data/adr-sweep-results.md`, every commit SHA recorded): **46.5% pooled (ADR-weighted), 56.6% per-repo mean** — the two weightings bracket the informal "~52%" figure, which is thus consistent with the population. The median per-repo median commit count per ADR is 1. Write-once is therefore not neglect but the expected shape of a decision record.

## 4. Design implication

If the derivable half must not be stored and the decision half's only reliable link is the forward one, the minimal honest system is:

1. **A decision ledger.** Append-only records of non-derivable intent. Forward links only. Back-links **derived** by scanning — as Datomic derives reverse references, as Git derives a commit's children, as double-entry bookkeeping derives balances. Because the back-link is computed, the reciprocity gap of §3 cannot exist by construction. Supersession resolved by `max(serial)` in code, never by an LLM's judgment of which fact is newer.
2. **A linter, not a certifier.** It verifies that each fully-qualified code anchor (`repo/path/File:Symbol`) resolves — structural drift is cheap to catch and worth gating. It never asserts the prose is true: a resolving anchor proves the file exists, not that the claim about it holds, and a validated anchor makes a stale claim sound *more* authoritative. Detection of structural drift is solved (~90%+ in the literature); semantic verification is not, and is left to a human.

We do **not** store: a regenerable cache of the code, typed `updated:` fields (git owns those), or stored back-links (derived). The residue is ~330 lines of shell (`bin/anchor-check`, `bin/ledger`), with a self-test whose every control is paired with its falsifier.

## 5. Threats to validity

- The §3 corpora are self-selected toward systems that *have* a supersession convention; systems without one contribute no data. The asymmetry claim is about maintenance of an existing convention, not its adoption.
- Anchor resolution depends on fully-qualified paths; symbol identity across refactors is only approximable (best published trackers reach ~97–99% F1 on curated oracles, and one 2025 result found predecessor oracles themselves contained errors). We therefore treat drift as budgeted maintenance, not a solvable-away bug.
- Numbers marked [UNVERIFIED] came from an automated research pass; two figures from that pass were already found wrong on first-hand recheck (a KEP field count; a status-field count), which is precisely why every load-bearing number in this note sits behind a script.

## 6. Conclusion

The interesting move is not a mechanism but a cut: the line between what a machine can re-derive and what only a human decided. Everything derivable wants to be recomputed, not stored; every decision wants to be stored once and never touched. Decades of systems ran that line through the middle of a single artifact and spent themselves keeping both halves in sync. Do not keep them in sync — keep them apart.

## Reproducibility

All numbers: `data/*.py` against live public datasets; tools: `bin/*`; self-test: `./test.sh`. Re-run and you get the same answer, or a newer one.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# ledger — the decision half. Write-once records of the non-derivable "why".
#
# The whole thesis of this repo, in one executable:
#   * A decision is stored ONCE and never edited. It is superseded, not changed.
#   * Only the FORWARD link is written ("this supersedes N"), by the author who
#     is already editing their own new record.
#   * The BACK link ("what superseded me") is NEVER stored — it is DERIVED by
#     scanning, exactly like git derives a commit's children. Storing it would
#     mean mutating an old, immutable record every time something points at it.
#   * "Which decision is current" is resolved by max(serial) in code — never by
#     asking a model which fact is newer. (The one benchmark built to test that
#     found deterministic resolution beats LLM judgment by 10+ points.)
#
# A decision is one Markdown file: NNNN-slug.md, NNNN a zero-padded serial.
# Frontmatter carries ONLY non-derivable fields. No `superseded_by:` — that's
# derived. No `updated:` — git owns that.
#
#   ---
#   id: 0007
#   title: FAQ owns its items
#   date: 2026-07-17
#   supersedes: [0003]
#   ---
#   We considered modelling FAQ as a content block with a naming convention.
#   Rejected: an FAQ owns ordered items; a content block is a single blob...
#
# Usage:
#   ledger init   <dir>
#   ledger new    <dir> "<title>" [--supersedes N[,N...]]
#   ledger show   <dir>               # current decisions (max-serial heads)
#   ledger show   <dir> --all         # every record, with DERIVED back-links
#   ledger check  <dir>               # supersession chains acyclic & single-headed
#   ledger redact <dir> N "<reason>"  # remove a record's CONTENT, keep its skeleton
#
# On redact: the WHY prose is replaced by a tombstone, but id/date/supersedes are
# preserved so the supersession chain and every DERIVED back-link stay intact.
# This is the one, deliberate, narrow exception to write-once — the GDPR /
# "recorded in error" path, designed in from the start rather than bolted on
# later (which is what every mature append-only system regretted). It is logged
# in the record itself; it never renumbers, never rewrites links.
#
# Deliberately tiny. Smallness is the point — see README.md.

set -euo pipefail

die() { echo "ledger: $*" >&2; exit 1; }

# --- frontmatter helpers (line-oriented; no YAML dependency) -----------------

# Print the value of a scalar frontmatter key from a file.
fm_get() {
  # $1 file, $2 key
  awk -v k="$2" '
    /^---[[:space:]]*$/ { n++; next }
    n==1 && $0 ~ "^"k":" { sub("^"k":[[:space:]]*",""); print; exit }
  ' "$1"
}

# Print serials listed in `supersedes: [a, b]` (space/comma separated), one per line.
fm_supersedes() {
  local raw
  raw="$(fm_get "$1" supersedes)"
  [ -n "$raw" ] || return 0
  echo "$raw" | tr -d '[]' | tr ',' ' ' | tr -s ' ' '\n' | sed '/^$/d'
}

records() {
  # emit every NNNN-*.md in serial order
  find "$1" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]-*.md' 2>/dev/null | sort
}

next_serial() {
  local last
  last="$(records "$1" | sed -E 's#.*/([0-9]{4})-.*#\1#' | tail -1)"
  [ -n "$last" ] || { echo "0001"; return; }
  printf '%04d' "$((10#$last + 1))"
}

slugify() {
  echo "$1" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed -E 's/[^a-z0-9]+/-/g; s/^-+|-+$//g' | cut -c1-50
}

# --- commands ----------------------------------------------------------------

cmd_init() {
  local dir="${1:?usage: ledger init <dir>}"
  mkdir -p "$dir"
  echo "ledger: initialized $dir"
}

cmd_new() {
  local dir="${1:?usage: ledger new <dir> \"<title>\" [--supersedes N]}"
  shift
  local title="${1:?title required}"; shift || true
  local sup=""
  while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
      --supersedes) sup="${2:?}"; shift 2 ;;
      *) die "unknown arg: $1" ;;
    esac
  done
  [ -d "$dir" ] || die "not a ledger dir: $dir (run: ledger init $dir)"

  local serial slug file supersedes_line="[]"
  serial="$(next_serial "$dir")"
  slug="$(slugify "$title")"
  file="$dir/$serial-$slug.md"

  if [ -n "$sup" ]; then
    # normalize "3" or "3,5" or "0003" -> [0003, 0005], and verify targets exist
    local norm="" s
    for s in $(echo "$sup" | tr ',' ' '); do
      s="$(printf '%04d' "$((10#$s))")"
      records "$dir" | grep -q "/$s-" || die "supersedes target not found: $s"
      norm="${norm:+$norm, }$s"
    done
    supersedes_line="[$norm]"
  fi

  # date passed in is avoided (no clock in this script's contract); use git-free stamp
  local today; today="$(date +%Y-%m-%d 2>/dev/null || echo 'YYYY-MM-DD')"

  cat > "$file" <<EOF
---
id: $serial
title: $title
date: $today
supersedes: $supersedes_line
---

<!-- The non-derivable WHY. What was considered and rejected, and the constraint
     that forced the call. This file is write-once: never edit it, supersede it. -->

EOF
  echo "$file"
}

# Build the DERIVED back-link map: for each serial, who supersedes it.
# Printed as "SERIAL SUPERSEDER" lines. This is never stored.
_derive_backlinks() {
  local dir="$1" f id t
  while IFS= read -r f; do
    [ -n "$f" ] || continue
    id="$(fm_get "$f" id)"
    for t in $(fm_supersedes "$f"); do
      t="$(printf '%04d' "$((10#$t))")"
      echo "$t $id"
    done
  done < <(records "$dir")
}

cmd_show() {
  local dir="${1:?usage: ledger show <dir> [--all]}"; shift || true
  local all=0
  [ "${1:-}" = "--all" ] && all=1
  [ -d "$dir" ] || die "not a ledger dir: $dir"

  local backlinks; backlinks="$(_derive_backlinks "$dir")"

  local f id title superseded_by
  while IFS= read -r f; do
    [ -n "$f" ] || continue
    id="$(fm_get "$f" id)"
    title="$(fm_get "$f" title)"
    # DERIVE: is this record superseded by anyone?
    superseded_by="$(echo "$backlinks" | awk -v k="$id" '$1==k{print $2}' | paste -sd, - 2>/dev/null || true)"

    if [ -n "$superseded_by" ]; then
      [ "$all" -eq 1 ] && printf '  %s  %-40s  (superseded by %s)\n' "$id" "$title" "$superseded_by"
    else
      # no successor => current head
      printf '* %s  %-40s  [current]\n' "$id" "$title"
    fi
  done < <(records "$dir")
}

cmd_redact() {
  local dir="${1:?usage: ledger redact <dir> N \"<reason>\"}"
  local id="${2:?record id required}"
  local reason="${3:?reason required (this is logged in the record)}"
  [ -d "$dir" ] || die "not a ledger dir: $dir"

  id="$(printf '%04d' "$((10#$id))")"
  local file
  file="$(records "$dir" | grep "/$id-" | head -1)"
  [ -n "$file" ] || die "record not found: $id"

  grep -q '^redacted:' "$file" && die "already redacted: $id"

  local today; today="$(date +%Y-%m-%d 2>/dev/null || echo 'YYYY-MM-DD')"

  # Keep the frontmatter skeleton (id/title/date/supersedes drive derivation);
  # drop the body; stamp the redaction inside the record.
  local tmp; tmp="$(mktemp)"
  awk -v d="$today" -v r="$reason" '
    BEGIN { fm=0 }
    /^---[[:space:]]*$/ { fm++; print; if (fm==2){ print "redacted: " d " — " r } next }
    fm<2 { print; next }
    fm>=2 && !done { print ""; print "[REDACTED " d ": " r "]"; done=1 }
  ' "$file" > "$tmp"
  mv "$tmp" "$file"
  echo "redacted $id — skeleton and links preserved: $file"
}

# Verify the supersession graph is sane: acyclic, single-headed per chain.
cmd_check() {
  local dir="${1:?usage: ledger check <dir>}"
  [ -d "$dir" ] || die "not a ledger dir: $dir"
  local backlinks rc=0
  backlinks="$(_derive_backlinks "$dir")"

  # 1. every supersedes target must exist (new already enforces this; re-check)
  local f t
  while IFS= read -r f; do
    for t in $(fm_supersedes "$f"); do
      t="$(printf '%04d' "$((10#$t))")"
      records "$dir" | grep -q "/$t-" || { echo "BROKEN: $(basename "$f") supersedes missing $t" >&2; rc=1; }
    done
  done < <(records "$dir")

  # 2. no record superseded by more than one head (multi-headed chain = ambiguous current)
  local dup
  dup="$(echo "$backlinks" | awk '{c[$1]++} END{for(k in c) if(c[k]>1) print k}')"
  if [ -n "$dup" ]; then
    echo "AMBIGUOUS: record(s) superseded by multiple successors: $dup" >&2
    rc=1
  fi

  # 3. no self-supersession (cheapest cycle)
  echo "$backlinks" | awk '$1==$2{print} ' | while read -r a b; do
    echo "CYCLE: $a supersedes itself" >&2
  done
  echo "$backlinks" | awk '$1==$2' | grep -q . && rc=1

  [ "$rc" -eq 0 ] && echo "ledger check: chains acyclic, single-headed, all targets present."
  return $rc
}

# --- dispatch ----------------------------------------------------------------

cmd="${1:-}"; shift || true
case "$cmd" in
  init)   cmd_init   "$@" ;;
  new)    cmd_new    "$@" ;;
  show)   cmd_show   "$@" ;;
  check)  cmd_check  "$@" ;;
  redact) cmd_redact "$@" ;;
  ""|-h|--help)
    sed -n '2,40p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'
    ;;
  *) die "unknown command: $cmd (try: init|new|show|check)" ;;
esac
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# anchor-check — the immune system, not the certifier.
#
# Every doc anchor `repo/path/File.ext` or `repo/path/File.ext:Symbol` must
# resolve against the code: the file exists, and (if a symbol is named) the
# symbol appears in it. A broken anchor IS drift — caught the moment it happens.
#
# What this DOESN'T do, on purpose: it does not claim the doc is correct.
# A resolving anchor proves the file exists, not that the prose about it is true.
# A validated anchor makes a stale claim sound MORE authoritative, not less.
# So this flags; it never blesses. Detecting structural drift is cheap and worth
# gating in CI. Semantic truth is not machine-checkable — that stays a human's job.
#
# Usage:
#   anchor-check <docs-dir> <code-root>
#
# Example (this repo's test-bed — read-only, never modified):
#   anchor-check ../../COMPANY/wiki ../../COMPANY
#
# Exit: 0 if every anchor resolves, 1 if any is broken.

set -euo pipefail

DOCS="${1:?usage: anchor-check <docs-dir> <code-root>}"
CODE="${2:?usage: anchor-check <docs-dir> <code-root>}"

[ -d "$DOCS" ] || { echo "anchor-check: docs dir not found: $DOCS" >&2; exit 2; }
[ -d "$CODE" ] || { echo "anchor-check: code root not found: $CODE" >&2; exit 2; }

# An anchor is a backtick-quoted path with a source extension, optional :Symbol.
# Extend the extension list for your stack.
ANCHOR_RE='`[A-Za-z0-9_.][A-Za-z0-9_./-]*\.(cs|tsx|ts|js|jsx|sql|py|go|rs|java|rb)(:[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)?`'

# An anchor is repo-ROOTED when its first path segment is a real directory under
# the code root (e.g. `company.cms/...`). Only rooted anchors are addresses a
# machine can resolve; a bare `FaqDtos.cs` or `components/Foo.tsx` is a human
# mention, not an anchor. This distinction IS the point — an anchor must be a
# fully-qualified address, or it can't be a load-bearing link. We verify the
# rooted ones and report the unrooted ones as a discipline gap, not as drift.

rooted() {
  # $1 = anchor path (no :symbol). True if first segment is a dir under CODE
  # AND the path carries no `...` elision (an elided path is a human mention,
  # not a resolvable address).
  case "$1" in
    *...*) return 1 ;;             # elision => not a full address
    */*)   [ -d "$CODE/${1%%/*}" ] ;;
    *)     return 1 ;;            # single segment => bare basename, never rooted
  esac
}

total=0 ok=0 broken=0 unrooted=0
broken_list=""

# Harvest unique anchors across all markdown, strip the backticks.
anchors="$(grep -rhoE "$ANCHOR_RE" "$DOCS" --include='*.md' 2>/dev/null | tr -d '`' | sort -u || true)"

if [ -z "$anchors" ]; then
  echo "anchor-check: no anchors found under $DOCS" >&2
  exit 0
fi

while IFS= read -r anchor; do
  [ -n "$anchor" ] || continue

  # Split optional :Symbol. Colons are illegal in these paths, so last field is safe.
  path="${anchor%%:*}"
  symbol=""
  [ "$anchor" != "$path" ] && symbol="${anchor##*:}"

  if ! rooted "$path"; then
    unrooted=$((unrooted + 1))
    continue
  fi

  total=$((total + 1))
  file="$CODE/$path"

  if [ ! -f "$file" ]; then
    broken=$((broken + 1))
    broken_list="${broken_list}  BROKEN(file)   $anchor"$'\n'
    continue
  fi

  if [ -n "$symbol" ]; then
    # Symbol must appear as a whole word somewhere in the file.
    if ! grep -qE "\\b${symbol}\\b" "$file" 2>/dev/null; then
      broken=$((broken + 1))
      broken_list="${broken_list}  BROKEN(symbol) $anchor"$'\n'
      continue
    fi
  fi

  ok=$((ok + 1))
done <<EOF
$anchors
EOF

echo "rooted anchors: $total | resolve: $ok | broken: $broken"
echo "unrooted mentions (not verifiable, discipline gap): $unrooted"

if [ "$broken" -gt 0 ]; then
  printf '\n%s' "$broken_list"
  echo "drift detected: $broken rooted anchor(s) fail to resolve." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "clean: every rooted anchor resolves."
```

# SOURCE: cache-and-ledger/data/README.md
# data — reproduce the numbers first-hand

The essay's central claim is that decision-record systems rot *asymmetrically*:
the forward link (written by an author already editing their doc) survives, the
back link (which forces an edit to an untouched document) does not — so you should
**derive the back link, not store it**. These two scripts check that claim against
live public datasets, so the numbers in `../README.md` are reproducible, not taken
on faith from a research pass. No dependencies beyond Python 3.

## PEP reciprocity

```
python3 verify-pep-reciprocity.py
```

Downloads `https://peps.python.org/api/peps.json` and computes, first-hand:

- forward `Replaces` reciprocity: **27/42 (64%)**
- back `Superseded-By` reciprocity: **27/32 (84%)**
- header/status mismatches: **10** PEPs

The weaker-reciprocated direction is the forward one — the direction that decays
is the one requiring you to edit a document you're not otherwise touching.

Offline: pass a saved copy — `python3 verify-pep-reciprocity.py --offline peps.json`.

## KEP field decay

```
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse \
    https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements.git ke
cd ke && git sparse-checkout set keps && cd ..
python3 verify-kep-decay.py ke/keps
```

Scans every `kep.yaml` line-wise (no PyYAML) and reports:

- **656** KEPs; **47** carry a non-empty `replaces:`; **50** forward values
- of those 50, **3 resolve** to a KEP; **47 are junk** (URLs, dead paths, `n/a`)
- **4** KEPs carry `status: replaced` (the stored back-state)

50 forward claims vs 4 stored back-states, and 94% of the forward values are
unresolvable freetext — a typed field that gates nothing decays. Note these came
out *sharper* than the original research pass (which reported "44 real"); that gap
is the entire reason these live behind a script instead of a citation.

## ADR write-once & supersede asymmetry

```
git clone https://github.com/adr/madr.git
git clone https://github.com/arachne-framework/architecture.git arachne
python3 verify-adr-writeonce.py madr    'docs/decisions/*.md'
python3 verify-adr-writeonce.py arachne 'adr-*.md'
```

Counts commits per ADR (write-once == 1 commit) and inspects status/supersede
references. Findings, first-hand:

Two example repos (both actively maintained, hence *low* write-once):
- **MADR** (the dominant template): 19 ADRs, only **3 carry a status field**; and
  `0008-add-status-field.md` itself carries `status: on hold`.
- **Arachne** (the canonical showcase): 16 ADRs, 100% status, forward 1 / back **0**.

**Population sweep** (see `adr-sweep-results.md` for the full 67-repo table and SHAs):

```
67 repos, 765 ADRs
write-once:  46.5% pooled (ADR-weighted) | 56.6% per-repo mean   → "~52%" confirmed
status field: 68% pooled
supersede:   50 forward vs 22 back = 2.3 : 1  (back maintained in 16/67 repos)
```

The load-bearing, reproduced result across PEP + KEP + ADR: **the forward reference
outnumbers the maintained back reference in every regime** — from 64% reciprocity
under a CI linter (PEP) to near-total decay where nothing gates the field (KEP), to
a moderate 2.3:1 in ordinary ADR repos. It is *never* fully reciprocal, so: derive
the back link, don't store it. (Note: this 2.3:1 corrects an earlier pass that
reported the ADR gap as an order of magnitude — one of three such corrections this
sweep and its siblings produced.)

## The discipline

An LLM asserting a number is confident fabrication with no epistemic state for
"I didn't actually check." The only defense is to make the check cheap and
reproducible. A number without a script here is a claim, not a fact.

input.new_string:
"""Deterministic isnad parser + mention-matching metrics for the GiraffeGraph pilot.

Scope: Arabic hadith text (Sanadset 650K, CC0). No LLM. Two jobs:
  1. rule_parse(raw)  -> ordered list of narrator-mention strings
  2. score(ref, hyp)  -> mention-level P/R/F1 under strict and lenient matching,
                         plus chain-order and ungrounded-mention diagnostics
"""
import re
import unicodedata
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- normalisation
HARAKAT = re.compile(r"[\u0610-\u061A\u064B-\u065F\u0670\u06D6-\u06ED\u0640]")
PUNCT = re.compile(r"[،.؛:!؟\"'()\[\]{}«»\-–—/\\*·]")


def norm(s: str) -> str:
    """Diacritic- and orthography-insensitive Arabic form used for matching."""
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", s)
    s = HARAKAT.sub("", s)
    s = PUNCT.sub(" ", s)
    s = re.sub(r"[أإآٱ]", "ا", s)
    s = s.replace("ى", "ي").replace("ة", "ه").replace("ؤ", "و").replace("ئ", "ي")
    s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()
    return s


HONORIFIC = re.compile(
    r"(رضي الله عنهما|رضي الله عنها|رضي الله عنهم|رضي الله عنه|"
    r"صلى الله عليه وسلم|عليه السلام|عليها السلام|رحمه الله|"
    r"ام المومنين|المومنين)"
)
# leading conjunction / siga residue that Sanadset itself sometimes keeps
LEAD_JUNK = re.compile(r"^(و|ف|ثم|قال|قالت|يقول|انه|انها|ان)\s+")


def clean_mention(s: str) -> str:
    s = norm(s)
    s = HONORIFIC.sub(" ", s)
    s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()
    for _ in range(3):
        s2 = LEAD_JUNK.sub("", s)
        if s2 == s:
            break
        s = s2
    return s.strip()


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ siga lexicon
# Transmission verbs (tahammul/ada' formulae). Order matters: longest first.
SIGA = [
    "حدثنا", "حدثني", "حدثناه", "حدثنيه", "اخبرنا", "اخبرني", "انبانا", "انباني",
    "نبانا", "نباني", "حدثهم", "حدثه", "اخبرهم", "اخبره", "سمعت", "سمعنا",
    "قرات علي", "قرا علينا", "عرضت علي", "كتب الي", "فيما قرا", "ذكر لنا",
    "ثنا", "انا", "عن", "ان",
]
SIGA_RE = re.compile(r"(?:^|\s)(" + "|".join(sorted(SIGA, key=len, reverse=True)) + r")(?=\s|$)")

# Markers that the chain has ended and the matn has begun.
MATN_CUE = re.compile(
    r"(رسول الله|النبي|صلي الله عليه وسلم|قال\s*:|قالت\s*:|"
    r"انه قال|انها قالت|يقول\s*:|سالت|بلغه|نهي|امر\s*ب)"
)
# tahwil marker: a bare 'ح' separating parallel chains
TAHWIL = re.compile(r"(?:^|\s)ح(?=\s|$)")

STOP_TOKENS = {
    "الله", "رسول", "النبي", "قال", "قالت", "قالوا", "يقول", "انه", "انها",
    "ان", "عن", "في", "علي", "الي", "من", "مثله", "بهذا", "الاسناد", "نحوه",
    "جميعا", "كلاهما", "كلهم", "وهو", "يعني", "هو", "بن", "بنت",
}


def _looks_like_name(tok_list) -> bool:
    if not tok_list:
        return False
    content = [t for t in tok_list if t not in STOP_TOKENS]
    return len(content) >= 1


def rule_parse(raw: str, max_mentions: int = 40):
    """Sigha-driven isnad segmentation. Returns ordered narrator mentions."""
    text = norm(raw)
    # keep every parallel chain: split on tahwil, parse each side
    chunks = [c for c in TAHWIL.split(text) if c.strip()]
    out = []
    for chunk in chunks:
        # cut the chunk at the first matn cue that follows at least one siga
        first_siga = SIGA_RE.search(chunk)
        if first_siga is None:
            continue
        cue = MATN_CUE.search(chunk, first_siga.end())
        isnad = chunk[: cue.start()] if cue else chunk
        tail = chunk[cue.start():] if cue else ""
        # a second isnad can start inside the tail (new hadith / follow-up chain)
        pieces = [isnad]
        while tail:
            nxt = SIGA_RE.search(tail)
            if nxt is None:
                break
            sub = tail[nxt.start():]
            cue2 = MATN_CUE.search(sub, nxt.end() - nxt.start())
            pieces.append(sub[: cue2.start()] if cue2 else sub)
            tail = sub[cue2.start():] if cue2 else ""
        for piece in pieces:
            spans = [m.span(1) for m in SIGA_RE.finditer(piece)]
            for i, (s, e) in enumerate(spans):
                nxt_start = spans[i + 1][0] if i + 1 < len(spans) else len(piece)
                cand = piece[e:nxt_start]
                # 'و' introduces a co-narrator: split it out as its own mention
                for part in re.split(r"(?:^|\s)و(?=\s)", cand):
                    m = clean_mention(part)
                    toks = m.split()
                    if not _looks_like_name(toks):
                        continue
                    if len(toks) > 9:
                        toks = toks[:9]
                    out.append(" ".join(toks))
    # drop immediate repeats, cap length
    dedup = []
    for m in out:
        if not dedup or dedup[-1] != m:
            dedup.append(m)
    return dedup[:max_mentions]


# ------------------------------------------------------------------- matching
def tok_f1(a: str, b: str) -> float:
    A, B = set(a.split()) - STOP_TOKENS, set(b.split()) - STOP_TOKENS
    if not A or not B:
        A, B = set(a.split()), set(b.split())
    if not A or not B:
        return 0.0
    inter = len(A & B)
    if inter == 0:
        return 0.0
    p, r = inter / len(A), inter / len(B)
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r)


def sim(a: str, b: str, mode: str) -> float:
    if mode == "strict":
        return 1.0 if a == b else 0.0
    # lenient: substring containment or token-F1 >= .6
    if a == b:
        return 1.0
    if a and b and (a in b or b in a):
        return 0.9
    f = tok_f1(a, b)
    return f if f >= 0.60 else 0.0


def align(ref, hyp, mode):
    if not ref or not hyp:
        return [], 0.0
    M = np.zeros((len(ref), len(hyp)))
    for i, a in enumerate(ref):
        for j, b in enumerate(hyp):
            M[i, j] = sim(a, b, mode)
    ri, ci = linear_sum_assignment(-M)
    pairs = [(i, j) for i, j in zip(ri, ci) if M[i, j] > 0]
    return pairs, float(sum(M[i, j] for i, j in pairs))


def score_one(ref_raw, hyp_raw, source_raw, mode="lenient"):
    ref = [clean_mention(x) for x in ref_raw]
    hyp = [clean_mention(x) for x in hyp_raw]
    ref = [x for x in ref if x]
    hyp = [x for x in hyp if x]
    pairs, _ = align(ref, hyp, mode)
    tp = len(pairs)
    src = norm(source_raw)
    ungrounded = sum(1 for h in hyp if h and h not in src and tok_f1_in(h, src) < 0.9)
    # order: Kendall-style concordance over matched pairs
    order_ok = order_concordance(pairs)
    return {
        "n_ref": len(ref), "n_hyp": len(hyp), "tp": tp,
        "fp": len(hyp) - tp, "fn": len(ref) - tp,
        "ungrounded": ungrounded,
        "order_conc": order_ok,
        "pairs": pairs, "ref": ref, "hyp": hyp,
    }


def tok_f1_in(mention: str, src: str) -> float:
    toks = [t for t in mention.split() if t not in STOP_TOKENS]
    if not toks:
        return 0.0
    return sum(1 for t in toks if t in src) / len(toks)


def order_concordance(pairs):
    if len(pairs) < 2:
        return None
    seq = [j for _, j in sorted(pairs)]
    conc = dis = 0
    for a in range(len(seq)):
        for b in range(a + 1, len(seq)):
            if seq[b] > seq[a]:
                conc += 1
            else:
                dis += 1
    tot = conc + dis
    return conc / tot if tot else None


def aggregate(per_item):
    tp = sum(d["tp"] for d in per_item)
    fp = sum(d["fp"] for d in per_item)
    fn = sum(d["fn"] for d in per_item)
    ung = sum(d["ungrounded"] for d in per_item)
    nhyp = sum(d["n_hyp"] for d in per_item)
    P = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    R = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    F1 = 2 * P * R / (P + R) if P + R else 0.0
    F05 = (1.25 * P * R / (0.25 * P + R)) if (0.25 * P + R) else 0.0
    oc = [d["order_conc"] for d in per_item if d["order_conc"] is not None]
    return {"P": P, "R": R, "F1": F1, "F0.5": F05, "tp": tp, "fp": fp, "fn": fn,
            "ungrounded": ung, "ungrounded_rate": ung / nhyp if nhyp else 0.0,
            "order_conc": float(np.mean(oc)) if oc else None, "n_hyp": nhyp}


def bootstrap_ci(per_item, stat="F1", B=2000, seed=7):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = len(per_item)
    vals = []
    for _ in range(B):
        idx = rng.integers(0, n, n)
        vals.append(aggregate([per_item[i] for i in idx])[stat])
    return float(np.percentile(vals, 2.5)), float(np.percentile(vals, 97.5))

def parse_json(t):
    if not t: return None
    m = re.search(r"\{.*\}", t, re.S)

    s=m.group(0)
    for cand in (s, re.sub(r",\s*([}\]])", r"\1", s)):

        except Exception: pass
    return None

        if d is None:

        nodes=d.get("nodes") or []; rels=d.get("relations") or []
        items=[]
        for n in nodes:
            if not isinstance(n,dict): continue

            qn=PI.norm(q); nn=PI.clean_mention(name)

            if nn and qn:
                if nn in PI.norm(q): rec["name_in_quote"]+=1

            if pos<0: pos = src.find(nn) if nn else 10**6

def taxonomy(cond, hyps):
    per=results[(cond,"lenient")]
    fn_cat=Counter(); fp_cat=Counter(); ex=defaultdict(list)
    for s,h,d in zip(sample,hyps,per):
        ref=d["ref"]; hyp=d["hyp"]; pairs=dict(d["pairs"])
        src=PI.norm(s["raw"])
        mr=set(pairs); mh=set(pairs.values())
        for i,r in enumerate(ref):
            if i in mr: continue
            # missed: is it in a parallel chain (after first matn cue)?
            pos=src.find(r)
            cue=PI.MATN_CUE.search(src)
            if pos>=0 and cue and pos>cue.start(): c="miss:parallel/secondary chain (after first matn)"
            elif len(r.split())==1: c="miss:single-token name"
            elif pos<0: c="miss:reference form absent from text (label noise)"
            else: c="miss:other"
            fn_cat[c]+=1; ex[c].append((s["coll"],r))
        for j,hh in enumerate(hyp):
            if j in mh: continue
            if hh not in src: c="spurious:not a substring of source (fabrication/normalisation)"
            elif any(t in hh.split() for t in ["النبي","رسول","الله"]): c="spurious:Prophet/Allah as narrator"
            elif len(hh.split())>6: c="spurious:over-long span (siga/honorific bleed)"
            elif len(hh.split())==1: c="spurious:fragment (over-segmentation)"
            else: c="spurious:other span-boundary error"
            fp_cat[c]+=1; ex[c].append((s["coll"],hh))
    return fn_cat, fp_cat, ex

    print(" FN:", dict(fn)); print(" FP:", dict(fp))
    for k in list(fp)[:3]: print("   e.g.",k,"->",[e[1][:40] for e in ex[k][:3]])

per_base = results[("C1_LLM_generic","lenient")]
ntri = np.array([d["n_hyp"] for d in per_base]); ok = np.array([d["tp"] for d in per_base])
m = ntri>0
p_i = ok[m]/ntri[m]
print(f"pilot: mentions/hadith mean={ntri.mean():.2f} sd={ntri.std():.2f}; "
      f"per-hadith precision mean={p_i.mean():.3f} sd={p_i.std():.3f}")
mu,var = p_i.mean(), p_i.var(ddof=1)
# method-of-moments Beta
k = mu*(1-mu)/var - 1
a0,b0 = max(mu*k,0.5), max((1-mu)*k,0.5)
print(f"Beta MoM: a={a0:.2f} b={b0:.2f} (implied sd={np.sqrt(a0*b0/((a0+b0)**2*(a0+b0+1))):.3f})")
lam = ntri.mean()

def sim_power(n_hadith, delta, B=600, Bboot=400, seed=0):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); wins=0
    for b in range(B):
        k_i = np.maximum(1, rng.poisson(lam, n_hadith))
        pb  = rng.beta(a0,b0,n_hadith)
        pt  = np.clip(pb+delta, 0, 1)
        ok_b = rng.binomial(k_i, pb); ok_t = rng.binomial(k_i, pt)
        # cluster bootstrap on the paired difference of corpus-level precision
        idx = rng.integers(0,n_hadith,(Bboot,n_hadith))
        d = (ok_t[idx].sum(1)/k_i[idx].sum(1)) - (ok_b[idx].sum(1)/k_i[idx].sum(1))
        lo = np.percentile(d,2.5)
        if lo > 0: wins+=1
    return wins/B

grid={}
for n in [100,200,350,500]:
    for dl in [0.02,0.03,0.05,0.10,0.15]:
        grid[(n,dl)] = sim_power(n,dl,B=400,Bboot=300,seed=n*100+int(dl*100))
    print(f"n={n:4d} " + "  ".join(f"Δ={d:.2f}:{grid[(n,d)]:.2f}" for d in [0.02,0.03,0.05,0.10,0.15]))

<skill-metadata name="figure-style" source="anthropic" note="read-only — fork under a new name to modify" />

# Publication-Grade Figure Rules

*A checklist for correct, legible, internally-consistent scientific figures. This
skill does not impose a visual house style — frame, font, and palette are
parameters. Once loaded, call `apply_figure_style()` before plotting.*

## §0 Scope

**Load trigger** (same rule as the system prompt's "Publication-grade plots"
section): this skill is for **final-deliverable figures** — those shipping in a
report, paper, or export, or saved as an artifact the user will keep — not for
exploratory/intermediate plots (quick looks, EDA, sanity checks), which are
drawn plainly without it. Once loaded, "every plot" below means every plot you
render toward the deliverable.

§1–§3, §8, and §9 are **correctness** — they apply to every plot, in every
context, and have no aesthetic content. §4–§7 are **guidance** — defaults that
produce a clean result but that a deliberate alternative can override
(individual rules inside §4–§7 that state a factual/perceptual invariant — e.g.
§4.4 semantic-zero centering, §4.5 CVD, §6.9 leader anchoring — still bind). On
its own, this skill is the inner tier (make one plot good); `figure-composer`
and `paper-narrative` supply multi-panel and whole-paper context.

---

## §1 Data fidelity & self-consistency

**1.1 Excluded rows.** A row marked excluded or flagged in the source data is
either omitted entirely or drawn with a visually distinct open/hatched marker
and named in the key. It **never** enters a summary statistic plotted alongside
the included rows.

**1.2 Comparable conditions only.** Arms measured under non-comparable
conditions (different N, epoch budget, initialization, protocol) are not plotted
as visual peers. Separate them with a facet break or a marker on the label, and
state the difference once in the caption.

**1.3 Self-consistency.** Every key, threshold, and title inside the figure must
be satisfied by every plotted row. Before saving, walk each categorical outcome
label back to the rule that defines it; if a row's value contradicts its label
or the title, the figure is wrong, not the data.

**1.4 Claim-titles must be true.** A sentence-title (§5.1) is tested against
every category on the axis before rendering. If any contradicts it, qualify the
title ("on 3 of 4 pairs") or downgrade it to a description.

**1.5 State n and what was held fixed.** Every panel that draws a summary mark
states `n` and the unit of replication, and every small-multiple that holds a
variable fixed states the fixed value — in the panel or, when §2 budget is
tight, in the caption.

**1.6 Reference structure is reference.** A tree, ordering, or topology drawn as
*context* (a scale bar, a category strip) uses an established reference, not
one inferred from the plotted data. Infer the structure only when the structure
*is* the result.

**1.7 One number per claim.** A quantitative claim (runtime, accuracy, count)
has exactly one canonical value across every panel, caption, and the abstract.
Define what it measures and use that value everywhere.

---

## §2 Label economy — floor and ceiling

The figure shows the pattern; the **caption** carries the context. Design for a
general scientific reader, not the author.

**2.1 Floor (non-removable).** Every distinct mark, series, glyph, or comparator
must be identifiable from the figure alone. The caption explains *why it
matters*, not *what it is*. A label is non-removable if deleting it leaves a
reader asking "what is that?"; it is removable only if the question becomes "why
is that there?". Comparator labels name the thing ("prior method", "no joint
training"), never a bare role word ("baseline", "previous"). Any term a general
scientist can't parse gets a one-word gloss.

**2.2 Ceiling.** Per panel: title + axis labels + tick labels + series identity
(labeled once per row of small multiples) + at most 2–3 result annotations.
Count the strings; >6 beyond axes/ticks means you're over. The ceiling counts
*narrative* annotations (callouts, value labels, brackets) — identity labels are
floor, not budget.

**2.3 Move to the caption:** n=, what's-held-fixed, abbreviation expansions,
non-comparable footnotes, exclusion rationale, methodological caveats.

**2.4 Titles are takeaways.** A reader seeing only the title knows what the
panel shows. "Robust to gene dropout" passes; "Fewer genes" fails. Test: read it
aloud cold — if the listener asks "fewer genes *what*?", rewrite. For a row of
small multiples that vary one thing, drop per-panel titles for one row-header.

**2.5 Value-on-mark only for the headline number** — the one a reader would
quote. Everything else is read off the axis.

**2.6 When in doubt, delete the label and re-read.** If the message survives, it
stays deleted.

---

## §3 Axes, scales, small multiples

**3.1 Axis padding.** Axis limits clear the data by ≥ one marker radius on every
side; markers and text never touch a spine. `ax.margins(0.04)` after plotting,
or extend the limit past any annotation.

**3.2 Axis breaks over wasted range.** When data occupy <40 % of an axis, break
the axis or start it at the data floor with a clear non-zero tick. Never draw a
reference line, threshold, or annotation inside a broken-axis gap — the gap has
no coordinate.

**3.3 Log axes get human-readable ticks** — `10²`, `10³`, or `1k / 10k / 100k`,
not raw exponents. **Never** draw filled bars on a log-scaled value axis (bar
length encodes ratio to an arbitrary floor); use points + median tick instead.

**3.4 Shared axes across small multiples.** A row or column of small multiples
shows tick labels once (leftmost / bottommost panel); interior panels keep ticks
but drop labels. When the panels share a y-axis and differ only by x-variable,
render them as abutting subplots (`wspace≤0.06`) with one row-header title.

**3.5 Fill the box.** A panel's data envelope occupies ≥75 % of its allotted
rectangle. If a panel's natural aspect leaves dead bands, reshape the grid
(rowspan, stacked complementary panels) — don't pad the panel.

**3.6 Direction of goodness.** When higher- or lower-is-better is not obvious
from the axis label, place a small upright cue ("higher = better") in the
margin — once per row of panels, never per panel, and never only in the caption.
A directional glyph embedded in rotated text rotates with it; set the cue
upright.

**3.7 Physical width.** A single-row figure at 300 dpi fits the venue's
double-column width. Adding a schematic or labels does not push data panels narrower than
they were before.

---

## §4 Color

**4.1 Threading.** Once a color is bound to an entity (a method, a feature, a
condition), reuse that exact color for every mark representing that entity
across the figure — line, fill, marker, text, heatmap row. Color *is* the
cross-reference; a reader should never have to consult a legend twice.

**4.2 Limit hues.** Use as few distinct hues as the data require. When the
figure compares a focal series against others, make the focal series visually
dominant (saturated, heavier weight) and render comparators with lower visual
weight (desaturated, lighter, or thinner). The focal hue must not coincide with
any hue in a categorical palette used in the same figure. The focal series must
remain identifiable even when its mark is zero-width or coincident with others —
via outline, marker, or a light tinted band.

**4.3 Hierarchical categories.** When categories nest (groups within groups),
the outer level picks the hue family and the inner level samples within it.

**4.4 Continuous and diverging.** Use a perceptually uniform sequential map for
generic continuous values; a single-hue ramp for ordinal rank or size; a
diverging map for signed quantities — **always** centered at the semantically
meaningful zero (0, 1.0, or median), never the data midpoint.

**4.5 CVD safety.** Never rely on a red/green contrast for a binary or opposing
distinction. Any binary pair should remain distinguishable in deuteranopia
simulation. Reserve one alarm hue for error/anomaly/perturbation marks and do
not reuse it as a data-series color.

**4.6 Two palettes, two legends.** When a figure uses two categorical color
systems, each legend sits adjacent to the first panel where its palette applies.

---

## §5 Typography

**5.1 Sentence titles.** A panel title states the comparison in plain language,
regular weight, left-aligned. Metric names go on the axis, not in the title.

**5.2 Role-mapped size ladder.** A figure uses **at most three** font sizes,
mapped to *role* not space: titles/axis-labels/series-identity at the base size;
legend/annotation text one step down; tick labels one step further. Panel
letters are the only exception (bold, larger). If a label doesn't fit at its
role's size, fix the layout or shorten the text — don't reach for an
intermediate size. `apply_figure_style(sizes=(8,7,6))` sets the ladder.

**5.3 Nomenclature.** Species, gene, and variable names that scientific
convention italicizes are italicized. Abbreviated codes inherit the rule; expand
once on first appearance.

**5.4 Magnitude suffixes.** Large counts use `k / M / B` (`4.2B`, `120 kb`),
not comma-grouped full numerals.

**5.5 Numeric annotations.** On-mark numbers use at most 2 significant figures —
unless 2-sf rounding would make two distinct rows print the same value, in which
case show the digit that separates them. Text on a filled mark reaches ≥4.5:1
contrast; if it doesn't, place the text outside the mark.

**5.6 No internal codes.** Axis labels use plain-language names; codebase
abbreviations appear only in parentheses after the readable name or in the
caption. Comparator series are labeled with what they *are*, not a role word.

**5.7 Panel letters.** Bold, top-left, outside the axes box. Case follows the
target venue's convention; `panel_letter(ax, 'a', case=...)` handles either.

---

## §6 Chart-family guidance (by data shape)

**6.1 Categorical × numeric.** Show the distribution, not just the summary.
Chart choice follows n: jittered strip with a median tick for small n; box or
violin for large n; bar + overlaid raw points or bar + interval when the mean is
the message. The `errorbar='ci95'` interval is the t-distribution 95% CI of the
mean (half-width `t_{0.975,n−1}·s/√n`), so it is valid at small n. Error bars
and raw-point overlays are alternatives — showing both is usually redundant. A
category absent from a group is marked (`n.d.`, `—`, or a hatched ghost) at its
slot; an empty slot reads as zero. A zero-valued bar
gets a visible stub or dot at the baseline.

**6.2 Single-observation categories.** A filled dot with a thin neutral stem to
the semantic zero (lollipop). Value labels sit beside the dot.

**6.3 Continuous series.** Mean-per-x as a line with markers; individual runs as
thin translucent lines or points behind it. Label each series with direct text
at the right end of its line in preference to a legend box. Summary glyphs
(per-bin mean/median) use a shape that cannot be mistaken for a raw observation,
identical across series, drawn below the raw points in z-order.

**6.4 Distributions on shared support.** When two distributions overlap heavily,
stack them as small panels with a shared x-axis or use a ridgeline. Overlay only
when the separation is visually clear.

**6.5 Matrices.** When a heatmap is small enough to read (< ~200 cells), print
the value in every cell. State the threshold once in the colorbar label.

**6.6 Embeddings.** Dimensionality-reduction scatters (UMAP, t-SNE, PCA) drop
ticks and tick labels; a small corner arrow pair names the axes. Clusters are
labeled by thin leader lines to text in surrounding whitespace.

**6.7 Paired prediction vs. observation.** Stack the two as adjacent tracks with
identical x and color; let the alignment carry the comparison. Target regions
are translucent spans registered in the legend.

**6.8 Insets.** Connect a detail inset to its source region visibly — a bounding
box with connector lines, or a translucent wedge.

**6.9 Label the extremes.** On a scatter of named observations, direct-label at
least the maximum, minimum, and any flagged point with a thin leader line. After
rendering, verify every leader endpoint terminates within one marker radius of
the row it names.

---

## §7 Layout & narrative

**7.1 Show what is measured before the result.** A reader should grasp what's
being compared before seeing the comparison — via a plain-language title, a
labeled schematic, or panel ordering. Any schematic uses the same words and
glyphs as the data panels' labels.

**7.2 One figure, one message.** A multi-panel figure has a single sentence it
is trying to make true. Every panel either states it, supports it, or bounds it;
panels that do none of these belong in supplement.

**7.3 Legends live in whitespace.** Frameless, placed inside the figure's
natural whitespace, or replaced by direct labeling. Legend entries are
swatch-first, left-aligned, and resolve every visually distinct glyph on the
panel.

**7.4 Row-band headers for nested faceting.** When small multiples are grouped,
each group gets one spanning header, not repeated per-panel titles.

**7.5 The figure arc.** For a paper: Figure 1 renders the paper's one-sentence
pitch as data — scope, not architecture. Subsequent figures cover mechanism,
evidence, robustness, application. A panel is judged against the paper's pitch,
not just its own figure's claim; content moves between figures if that's where
the story needs it. (`paper-narrative` runs this review.)

**7.6 Don't re-decorate a passing panel.** Between revision rounds, a panel that
already passes is not made more visually complex to fix nothing. Adding marks or
labels to a clean panel is a regression.

---

## §8 Anti-patterns

These are correctness failures, not style preferences:

- Red and green as opposing categories.
- Filled bars on a log-scaled value axis.
- Colorbar ticks that are evenly spaced but miss the semantic center.
- A diverging colormap whose center is the data midpoint, not the semantic zero.
- An axis title that restates the tick labels.
- Explaining the direction of goodness only in the caption.
- A "reference" line drawn at a value that is itself one of the plotted points.
- An excluded row that enters a plotted summary statistic.
- A leader line whose nearest mark is not the row it labels.

---

## §9 Render-then-verify

After `fig.savefig(...)`, before `save_artifacts`:

**9.1 Geometric (bbox) check.**
```python
r = fig.canvas.get_renderer()
texts = [(t, t.get_window_extent(r)) for t in fig.findobj(mpl.text.Text)
         if t.get_text().strip() and t.get_visible()]
spines = [(s, s.get_window_extent(r)) for ax in fig.axes
          for s in ax.spines.values() if s.get_visible()]
ticklabels = {ax: set(ax.get_xticklabels(which='both') + ax.get_yticklabels(which='both'))
              for ax in fig.axes}
overlaps  = [(a, b) for i, (a, ba) in enumerate(texts) for b, bb in texts[i+1:] if ba.overlaps(bb)]
overlaps += [(t, s) for t, bt in texts for s, bs in spines
             if bt.overlaps(bs) and t not in ticklabels[s.axes]]
# assert: overlaps == [] and every text box lies within fig.bbox
```
Overlap is defined between *visible* boxes, and a tick label sitting on its own
spine is not a finding. Fix (move, shorten, stagger) and re-save until clean.

**9.2 Perceptual check.** The bbox check is geometric, not perceptual — it will
not catch a low-contrast label, a leader that crosses three others, or a series
color mistakable for another. Crop the saved PNG to each panel and look:
```python
fig.savefig("figure.png")
for letter, box in panel_crops(fig).items():
    host.view_image("figure.png", crop=box)
```
For each crop: Is every glyph and mark legible against its background? Does the
smallest plotted element have a stroke or stub? Do any leaders cross? Could any
series color be mistaken for another? Does the legend sit beside what it keys?
A perceptual defect that passes §9.1 is still a defect.

---
*When in doubt: fewer hues, more direct labels, raw data over summary stats, and
state what is being measured before showing the result.*
